structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg and rents a modest bungalow between two lavish estates, feeling a sense of belonging after guiding a stranger to West Egg village. He drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a Yale acquaintance, where he meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker. During dinner, Tom aggressively promotes racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, and a phone call from his mistress in New York exposes his infidelity, which Jordan confirms in hushed tones; Daisy responds with performative cheer, fabricating a nightingale’s song, then privately tells Nick she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' Later, alone in his yard, Nick observes Gatsby standing on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay, trembling in silent reverence before vanishing into the night. This moment follows Nick’s reflective admission that, despite his disillusionment with the moral chaos of the East, Gatsby alone remains exempt from his cynicism due to his extraordinary gift for hope.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway accompanies Tom Buchanan by train from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forcibly pulls Nick from the train to meet Myrtle Wilson, his mistress, at her husband George B. Wilson’s run-down garage. Myrtle, distinct from her listless husband, travels separately by train to New York to avoid detection, then purchases an Airedale puppy for $10 and cosmetics at the station before arriving at a rented apartment on 158th Street. There, Tom retrieves whisky from a locked bureau, and Nick becomes drunk for the second time in his life; Myrtle transforms into a haughty social climber, donning a cream-coloured chiffon dress, and hosts a rowdy gathering with her sister Catherine and the photographer Mr. McKee and his wife. Conversations turn abrasive as Myrtle boasts about her affair with Tom, falsely claims Daisy Buchanan is a Catholic who refuses divorce, and defiantly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose with his open hand, triggering chaos, bloodshed, and stunned silence. Overwhelmed, Nick exits with the dazed Mr. McKee, rides the elevator down, and later falls asleep on a cold bench at Pennsylvania Station, awaiting the dawn train, haunted by the grotesque spectacle.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation from Jay Gatsby and arriving at Gatsby’s opulent mansion on Long Island late Saturday evening, where he is immersed in a lavish party featuring orchestral music, endless cocktails, catered feasts, and guests arriving by Rolls-Royce and station wagon. Amid the chaos, he overhears wild rumors about Gatsby—such as that he killed a man or was a German spy—meets Jordan Baker, encounters a drunken man in the library who is astonished to find the books are real, and speaks with a war veteran who invites him to fly in a hydroplane, yet still has not met Gatsby. Later, while drinking champagne at a table, Nick Carraway is shocked when the man beside him reveals himself as Gatsby, who warmly invites him to fly the next morning; Jordan is then summoned for a private hour-long conversation with Gatsby, leaving her cryptically intrigued. As the party descends into disorder—with a drunken woman crying with running ink, marital fights erupting, and a coupé crashing into a wall while the driver claims he wasn’t driving—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby standing alone, sober and formal, waving farewell under a faint moon as he departs. In a reflective interlude, Nick Carraway recounts his ordinary life in New York: working at the Probity Trust, lunching with clerks in dark restaurants, studying investments at the Yale Club while avoiding rowdy patrons, and walking home along Madison Avenue to Pennsylvania Station, where he imagines romantic encounters on Fifth Avenue; he reconnects with Jordan Baker, initially drawn by her fame as a golf champion, but becomes disillusioned upon learning she cheated in a tournament and lied about damaging a borrowed car, realizing her chronic dishonesty and his own emotional detachment from a woman back home, ultimately asserting he is one of the few honest people he knows.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a wild, glittering party attended by a vast array of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, including the Chester Beckers, Leeches, Blackbucks, Snells, Dancies, and Klipspringer, many arriving by car amid chaos—such as Ripley Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s automobile and Clarence Endive fighting a bum named Etty in the garden, while rumors circulate that Gatsby killed a man or is related to Von Hindenburg, yet no one knows his true identity. Later, on a late July morning, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and during the drive reveals an elaborate, contradictory life story—including wealthy Midwestern parents from San Francisco, Oxford education, European travels, wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest with medals from Allied nations, and physical proof in the form of a Montenegrin medal inscribed 'Orderi di Danilo' and a photograph of himself at Trinity Quad, which unsettles Nick Carraway’s skepticism. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, a grotesque figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal at the old Metropole; after Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call, Wolfsheim praises Gatsby as a gentleman from 'Oggsford College' and discreet with women, only for Gatsby to shock Nick Carraway by confessing he fixed the 1919 World Series, moments before Nick introduces him to Tom Buchanan and Gatsby vanishes. On a quiet October day in 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, where their intense romantic moment left a lasting impression; years later, Jordan reveals Daisy’s lavish marriage to Tom Buchanan—with a $350,000 string of pearls—and her drunken breakdown on her wedding day clutching a letter demanding the pearls be returned, before disclosing that six weeks prior, Daisy recognized Gatsby’s name and woke Jordan in shock, realizing he was the same officer from her past. After leaving the Plaza Hotel, Jordan and Nick Carraway ride in a victoria through Central Park at twilight, where Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and that he now asks Nick Carraway to invite Daisy to tea as a discreet means of reunion, having meticulously avoided direct contact out of fear, leaving Nick Carraway emotionally moved before turning his attention to Jordan himself.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night, Nick returns to his West Egg home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but empty, with Gatsby nervously inviting him to Coney Island and later probing his finances before offering a secretive business opportunity, which Nick declines. The next day, Nick invites Daisy to tea, warning her not to bring Tom; as rain falls, Gatsby sends a man to cut Nick’s grass and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers. Daisy arrives in a large open car driven by Ferdie, and Gatsby, pale and trembling in the rain, enters the house where their reunion is stilted—marked by Gatsby nearly knocking over a clock and awkward silence—until Daisy’s tears and Gatsby’s sudden radiant calm transform the mood. Afterward, Gatsby joyfully shows Daisy his mansion, touring its opulent rooms including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, passing Mr. Klipspringer doing liver exercises, before overwhelming her with his collection of expensive shirts, which causes her to sob into the fabrics. As rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, revealing its lost symbolism, shows Nick a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful picture of himself in yachting attire, and shares clippings about Daisy; Klipspringer nervously plays piano as the storm rages and lights flicker across West Egg, until Nick observes Gatsby’s dazed realization that Daisy cannot fulfill his idealized dream, yet remains captivated by her voice, leaving him alone in the rain as Gatsby and Daisy are utterly absorbed in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, mistakenly believing him to be a public figure, as wild rumors—such as that he lives in a boat disguised as a house—have fueled his notoriety; the narrative then reflects on Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior, joined Cody’s vessel as steward, mate, and jailor for five years, absorbing wealth and habits, including abstaining from alcohol after witnessing Cody’s excesses, only to be cheated out of a $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye upon Cody’s death, leaving him with only the polished identity he had forged. Later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and finds Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrived on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but their cold indifference and Sloane’s hostility culminate in the woman’s invitation to supper being abruptly cut off, forcing them to leave just as Gatsby emerges in his car, hat in hand, ready to follow. That evening, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is both enchanted and appalled by the extravagance, dances with Gatsby, and attempts to explain his wealth by claiming he owns drugstores, while Tom grows suspicious and calls him a bootlegger; after the party, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway that Daisy didn’t enjoy herself and insists she must say, 'I never loved you,' to reclaim their lost past, as he walks among the discarded flowers and fruit rinds, desperately trying to recapture the moment five years earlier when he first kissed Daisy under the moonlight.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house in East Egg, where Gatsby, having replaced his servants with associates of Meyer Wolfsheim, is summoned under Daisy’s request. During lunch, Daisy openly declares her love for Gatsby in front of Tom, triggering a volatile confrontation in which Tom mocks Gatsby’s claim of attending Oxford and accuses him of bootlegging through drugstores linked to Wolfsheim, while Gatsby demands Daisy admit she never loved Tom. The group departs for New York in two cars—Gatsby driving his own vehicle and Tom taking Daisy in the coupé—stopping at Wilson’s garage under the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, where a sick and distraught George Wilson reveals he plans to take Myrtle away and asks about buying Tom’s old car, unaware Tom is Myrtle’s lover. At the Plaza Hotel, tensions explode in a stifling suite as Daisy, trembling, admits she once loved both men but cannot fully renounce Tom; Tom then orders Daisy and Gatsby to return to Long Island together in Gatsby’s car. Shortly after seven, Myrtle Wilson runs from the garage and is struck by a speeding yellow car that does not stop; Michaelis, witnessing the crash, describes the car as light green but is unsure, while the driver of another car stops nearby and returns to the scene. Tom and Nick arrive at the Valley of Ashes to find Myrtle’s body under a swinging yellow light, with Wilson in shock, and Tom insists he was not driving the yellow car, though he had been earlier that day; shaken, Tom breaks down in tears, calling the driver a coward. Later, Nick waits outside the Buchanan house, where Gatsby emerges from the shadows to confess Daisy was driving when Myrtle was killed, and he intends to take the blame, remaining outside all night to guard her. Nick secretly observes Tom and Daisy in the kitchen eating together with quiet intimacy, confirming their bond endures; Gatsby stands alone in the moonlight, watching over a house where Daisy has already chosen Tom.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive and finds him dejected, having seen Daisy briefly appear at her window before turning off the light. They search the dusty, musty house for cigarettes, smoking outside as the morning light shifts from grey to gold; Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid suspicion over Daisy’s car, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that she will choose him. He recounts his youth with Dan Cody and his first encounter with Daisy as a penniless officer, having misled her into believing he was of her social class, and later, in a poignant flashback, recalls his lonely journey by day-coach to Louisville after returning from France, revisiting places tied to her and reaching out desperately from the train as the city faded. On the same morning, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, orders the butler to bring calls to the pool, and retrieves a pneumatic mattress he never used all summer, declining help as he walks alone among yellowing trees. Nick Carraway, after a strained and unresolved phone call with Jordan Baker—who has left Daisy’s house for Southampton—and finding Gatsby’s line occupied by a long-distance call from Detroit, returns to the mansion to discover Gatsby dead in the pool, floating on the mattress, his body disturbed only by breeze and falling leaves; moments later, the gardener finds George Wilson’s body in the grass, having arrived on foot from West Egg after learning Gatsby’s name and believing him responsible for Myrtle’s death.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: In the aftermath of Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the grim scene at the mansion as police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm the grounds, while false narratives from Catherine and the coroner’s label of Wilson as a 'madman' erase any connection between Gatsby and Myrtle. Despite desperate attempts to contact Daisy, Tom, and Meyer Wolfsheim, all refuse to respond or attend the funeral—Daisy and Tom vanish without a trace, Wolfsheim declines citing 'important business' and a personal rule against involvement with death, and Klipspringer calls only to request his tennis shoes. Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, overwhelmed with grief and pride, sharing a worn photograph of Gatsby’s imagined house and a tattered copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing Gatsby’s childhood self-improvement schedule. At the funeral in a heavy drizzle, only Gatz, the minister, Nick Carraway, four or five servants, the postman, and the mysterious man with owl-eyed glasses—whom Nick Carraway does not know by name—are present; the man wipes his rain-blurred glasses, murmurs 'Amen to that' after hearing 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' and quietly calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Later, Nick Carraway encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary while emotionally recounting tears over dog biscuits left behind, leaving Nick Carraway feeling pity rather than anger. After selling his car and packing his belongings, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s abandoned house one final time, erasing an obscene word scrawled on the steps, then walks to the beach where he reflects on the vanished wilderness once seen by Dutch sailors, realizing Gatsby’s dream was already lost, and concludes with the metaphor of boats beaten back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, and becomes entangled in the lives of his wealthy cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a brash Yale alumnus with a mistress in the desolate Valley of Ashes. Through Daisy, Nick meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker, and soon becomes fascinated by their mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, whose lavish parties draw crowds but conceal his true identity. Nick learns that Gatsby’s fortune and mansion were acquired solely to rekindle a lost romance with Daisy, whom he met as a young officer in Louisville five years earlier. As Gatsby draws Nick into his world, he reveals a carefully constructed persona—Oxford-educated war hero, heir to immense wealth—though fragments of his past as James Gatz of North Dakota emerge, revealing a self-made man shaped by obsession and idealism. Nick, increasingly disillusioned by the moral decay of the East, finds himself uniquely moved by Gatsby’s extraordinary capacity for hope.

The rising tension culminates in a carefully orchestrated reunion between Gatsby and Daisy at Nick’s home, where their emotional reconnection reignites Gatsby’s dream of reclaiming the past. But when Tom confronts Gatsby at the Plaza Hotel, the fragile illusion shatters: Daisy admits she once loved both men but cannot abandon Tom, and Gatsby’s fabricated identity is exposed as a product of bootlegging and criminal ties through Meyer Wolfsheim. The group departs in chaos, and shortly after, Myrtle Wilson is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy, though Gatsby takes the blame to protect her. Tom, knowing the truth, directs the grieving Myrtle’s husband George Wilson to Gatsby, falsely implicating him as both Myrtle’s lover and killer. Meanwhile, Nick watches helplessly as Gatsby clings to the hope that Daisy will leave Tom, even as she retreats into the safety of her marriage, leaving Gatsby alone in the moonlight, guarding a house that no longer belongs to his dream.

After Gatsby is shot and killed by Wilson in his pool, Nick struggles to organize a funeral, only to find that none of Gatsby’s so-called friends—Daisy, Tom, Wolfsheim, Klipspringer—will attend. Gatsby’s father arrives from Minnesota, proud of the son he barely knew, holding onto a photograph and a child’s schedule of self-improvement that reveals Gatsby’s lifelong pursuit of reinvention. At the sparse funeral, only a handful of people remain: Nick, Gatsby’s father, a few servants, and the mysterious owl-eyed man who quietly calls him 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick later confronts Tom, who admits he told Wilson about Gatsby’s car but feels no remorse, justifying it as necessary. Devastated by the emptiness of the world he has witnessed, Nick sells his car, abandons New York, and returns to the Midwest, reflecting on Gatsby’s dream as a metaphor for the American ideal—forever reaching toward a green light that recedes with every advance, boats beaten back ceaselessly into the past.
